title: Memory Consolidation
subtitle: Stabilising experiences across time and sleep
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating memory consolidation across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain memory consolidation in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in memory consolidation.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to memory consolidation.

sections.explainSimply: After an event, memories continue to change as they are stabilised and integrated.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Sleep, rehearsal, emotion and later information influence consolidation, so memory is reconstructive rather than a fixed recording.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Systems consolidation redistributes dependence across hippocampal–cortical networks over time, although models remain under debate.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of memory consolidation as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need memory consolidation to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Treatment should not promise to erase a memory.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use memory consolidation to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses memory consolidation to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Treatment should not promise to erase a memory. Evidence classification: established principle; evolving models.
